intro:
The best phone for restaurant use is usually a simple business line with reliable forwarding, a clear speaker or headset setup, and a phone host process that fits your shifts. The right setup is the one your team can use without thinking.

For many independent restaurants, the real question is not “Which phone is best?” It is “How do I answer calls fast, keep orders accurate, and avoid tying up the counter?” That is where a clean setup matters, whether you use staff, forwarding rules, or [ROAL](/how-it-works) for pickup and delivery calls.

sections.h2: What do restaurant owners need from a phone setup?
sections.body:
A restaurant phone has one job: get the call handled quickly and correctly. That means the phone should be easy to answer, easy to forward, and easy to hear over kitchen noise. If you take pickup orders, it also needs to support a headset or speaker so the person answering can keep both hands free.

Here is a practical checklist for the **best phone for restaurant** use:
- Clear audio in a noisy front counter or kitchen.
- A headset or speaker option for order taking.
- Easy call forwarding when the line is busy or closed.
- Separate handling for questions, reservations, and order calls.
- A setup your team can learn in one shift.

If you run a small pizza shop or deli, you do not need a complicated system. A stable business line plus a headset is often enough. If you want calls answered when you are slammed, [ROAL](/try) can answer the phone, take orders from your live menu, and send the ticket to the kitchen screen. It also hands off allergy-sensitive questions, complaints, and manager requests to staff with a summary.

sections.h2: Should you buy a desk phone, cordless phone, or headset system?
sections.body:
The right hardware depends on where the phone gets answered. In many restaurants, the counter person needs one of three setups.

| Setup | Best for | Good points | Watch-outs |
|---|---|---|---|
| Desk phone | Front counter with one main spot | Simple, familiar, reliable | Staff must stay near the phone |
| Cordless phone | Larger dining room or kitchen movement | Easy to carry around | Can be misplaced during rushes |
| Headset on a phone or computer | Busy takeout and pickup counters | Hands-free order taking | Needs a comfortable fit and clear volume |

A simple way to choose:
1. If one person answers most calls, start with a desk phone.
2. If staff move around a lot, use a cordless phone.
3. If one person takes calls while packing bags, use a headset.
4. If calls are routed to [ROAL](/use-cases/pickup-orders), the hardware burden drops because the phone host can handle the first conversation.

Example: say your front counter staff takes 20 calls in a busy dinner hour. A headset may save them from picking up and putting down a handset every few minutes. Plug in your own call count and see what keeps the line moving.

sections.h2: How do you forward calls without making a mess?
sections.body:
Forwarding is one of the most important parts of a restaurant phone setup. You want a rule that is easy for staff to understand: ring the shop first, then forward when busy, unanswered, or closed.

Many carriers and phone systems use different codes or portal settings, so always confirm with your carrier and test with a real call. Common examples include:
- Many landlines and some carriers: dial *72 plus the forwarding number to forward all calls, and *73 to turn it off.
- Some GSM mobile carriers: **21*number# forwards all calls and ##21# turns it off.
- Some carriers also use **61*number# for unanswered calls and **67*number# for busy calls.
- Verizon Wireless often uses *72 / *73, and *71 for busy/no-answer forwarding.
- Business VoIP systems usually set forwarding in the web portal.

A basic restaurant rule might look like this:
1. Ring the main line during open hours.
2. Forward to staff only when busy.
3. Forward to the phone host after close.
4. Turn forwarding off when the rush ends.

ROAL gives each location its own phone line automatically, and you can forward your existing number to it. The restaurant keeps its own number, and forwarding can be turned off any time.

sections.h2: What phone features matter most for order taking?
sections.body:
For restaurants, the useful features are not fancy. They are practical. You want clear caller ID, easy hold, fast transfer, and a way to write down order details without confusion.

Here is a short order-taking checklist:
- Ask for the caller’s name and phone number.
- Confirm size, modifiers, and special notes.
- Repeat the order back before ending the call.
- Quote a ready time.
- Mark sold-out items as unavailable.

A good phone setup also helps staff keep the line calm. A simple script line can be: "Thanks for calling. What can I get started for you today?" Then the staff member or phone host can move through the order in the same order every time.

If you use ROAL, it can take items, sizes, modifiers, notes, and the caller’s name and phone. It also speaks the caller’s language, which helps when your neighborhood gets a mix of customers. It does not take card numbers over the phone, so payment still happens at pickup or however your restaurant already handles it.

sections.h2: How much should you spend on phone hardware and services?
sections.body:
Phone cost is only one part of the equation. You should compare the cost of hardware, staff time, and missed calls. Some restaurants spend too much on a phone system that looks modern but still leaves the counter overloaded.

Here is a simple way to compare options using example numbers you can swap for your own:

| Cost item | Example | What to replace with your number |

| Monthly AI phone plan | $79 to $599 per location | Your quoted monthly fee |

Say you get 120 completed phone orders in a month. At $0.90 per completed order, that would be $108 for ROAL, plus any hardware you choose. Plug in your own order count to see what fits your shop.

This matters because delivery apps commonly take roughly 15-30% commission per order, which can be much harder to absorb on a $20 or $30 ticket. If you want to compare paths, [Pricing](/pricing) and [AI phone host vs delivery apps](/compare/delivery-apps) are useful starting points.

sections.h2: What should the phone flow look like during busy shifts?
sections.body:
A busy restaurant phone flow should be simple enough for a new employee to follow. The goal is to avoid long holds, missed details, and order mistakes.

Use this flow for a dinner rush:
1. Answer with the restaurant name.
2. Ask whether the caller wants pickup, delivery, or a question.
3. Take the order or transfer the issue.
4. Repeat the order back.
5. Quote the ready time.
6. Send the order to the kitchen or hand it to staff.

A practical script helps a lot. Example: "Thanks for calling Maria’s. Are you ordering pickup today, asking a menu question, or making a reservation?" That one line keeps the call moving.

ROAL is built around this kind of flow. It answers the phone, reads the live menu, takes pickup and delivery orders, answers common questions about hours, address, parking, and menu items, and sends a clean ticket to the kitchen screen. Questions it cannot answer go to an inbox, so the owner can respond once and the phone host knows it from then on.

sections.h2: How do you choose the simplest setup for your restaurant type?
sections.body:
The best phone setup depends on your format. A pizzeria, deli, family diner, or takeout spot does not need the same hardware mix.

Use this quick matching guide:
- **Pizza shop:** one front counter phone, headset, strong forwarding rules.
- **Deli or sandwich shop:** compact desk phone, easy hold, fast call-back.
- **Family restaurant:** one main line with clear reservation and takeout handling.
- **Multi-location group:** separate phone flows by location and a shared menu process.

If you want a no-stress setup, start with what you already have and tighten the process. Check your hours, voicemail, forwarding rules, and headset comfort. Make sure staff know exactly when to answer and when to let calls roll to the phone host.

ROAL can help here because setup starts from your website, Google Maps link, or your restaurant name and city. It reads menu, prices, hours, and address from public pages, and you can test-call it in the browser before you claim the host. If you want a free test host, you can [build a free test host](/try) once you are ready.

faq.q: Should a restaurant use call forwarding or a second phone line?
faq.a: Many restaurants use both. A second line can help separate dine-in, takeout, and reservations, while call forwarding lets you route calls when the line is busy or closed. The exact setup depends on your carrier or phone system, so confirm the codes and test them.
